author: Editorial
description:
A speech by the leader of the opposition exemplifies much that is wrong with the way British politics conventionally talks about benefit claimants

There is a big difference between expenditure that is rising and a rise that is “out of control”. The amount Britain spends on social security is in the former category. Too much political rhetoric around the subject assumes that it is in the latter one.

The Office for Budget Responsibility forecasts the growth in welfare spending over the next five years at 0.2%-0.5% of gross domestic product, from £353bn this year to £431bn in 2032. That money might well be suboptimally deployed. There are rival demands on the state’s resources and a reasonable debate to be had about priorities at the Department for Work and Pensions. But that is not the tone of the debate routinely conducted in Westminster.

Do you have an opinion on the issues rais
title: The Guardian view on welfare reform: time to retire lazy myths and stereotypes | Editorial

author: Nils Pratley
description:
National wealth fund is to lend £1bn towards the Vanguard projects – but whether the private equity giant needed help is debatable

“This major investment in UK renewables is a vote of confidence for building in Britain,” declared the prime minister.

Andy Burnham is obviously correct that the two Vanguard windfarms off the coast of Norfolk are huge investments. Together, they require almost £13bn of debt financing. But he can’t claim they represent a fresh expression of confidence. The project has been on the runway since the German utility RWE, the developer, was awarded a contract to build the windfarms in January’s renewables auction.
title: KKR and RWE are rich firms. Why do they need a UK state loan for their windfarms? | Nils Pratley

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Readers respond to reporting on the disgraced actor and comedian’s trial and conviction for rape and sexual assault

You report that in the wake of Russell Brand’s trial, the government pledged “to examine calls to crack down on ‘rape myths’ in trials” (Russell Brand suspected to have attacked at least 10 other women, 6 November). This is not the first time the treatment of women in trials for rape, and the perpetuation of rape myths, has been drawn to the attention of a Labour government.

Sue Lees (1941-2002), a former colleague from the Polytechnic/University of North London conducted research into the reporting of rape in the media and how it was treated within the English legal system in the 1990s.

Continue reading...
title: Russell Brand’s trial, rape myths and a questionable faith | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
One reader sounds a warning about all our devices that are connected to the internet, following a series of cyber-attacks on supermarket fridges

Well done to Alex Pearce for unplugging his fridge from the internet (Hot fridges, a fake nuclear alert and a $6bn heist: are we in the foothills of a hacking epidemic?, 8 November). My only question is why he didn’t do it a few weeks earlier, when the first round of hacked fridges were headline news for several days.

Your article notes that there are millions of devices connected to the internet. This sea of domestic and industrial controllers, known as the “internet of things” in marketing literature and the “internet of shit” by engineers, all have several thing
title: Hacked fridges and other dangers lurking in the ‘internet of shit’ | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Cow’s milk is not a natural source of iodine. It is fortified, at the cow, notes Dale Vince of the Green Britain Foundation

You report that scientists say moving even partly from dairy products to vegan alternatives could lead to deficiencies in iodine and other micronutrients if the substitutes are not fortified (Swapping from dairy to plant-based milk, cheese and yoghurt ‘could lead to micronutrient deficiencies’, 4 November).

To be clear, cow’s milk is not a natural source of iodine. It is fortified, at the cow. As the paper published in the Lancet Planetary Health explains, iodine is in milk because it is added to cattle feed. The vitamin B12 is there because cobalt is added to the feed so the
title: Clearing up confusion over iodine in milk | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
A reader highlights how the government’s immigration changes are affecting those who have been granted asylum and wish to apply for indefinite leave to remain

I am writing as a refugee who has lived in the UK since 2007. I claimed asylum in 2007, and my appeal was allowed by the first-tier tribunal (immigration and asylum) in February 2020. However, because of Home Office delays, I did not receive my five-year refugee permission until June 2022.

I applied for indefinite leave to remain in June 2025, but my application was refused because I had not completed five years from the date my refugee permission was granted. I was therefore expecting to apply again in June 2027.

Continue reading...
title: Asylum law changes are causing refugee families like mine terrible worry | Letter

author: Rowena Mason Whitehall editor
description:
Keir Starmer’s former chief of staff also says the ‘thicket of rules’ about how PMs operate should be cleared away

Keir Starmer’s former chief of staff, Morgan McSweeney, has called for a rethink of “quasi-judicial” powers given to cabinet ministers such as the energy secretary’s ability to approve future oil and gas fields.

McSweeney, who helped propel Starmer to power and served as his chief of staff until February this year, said he believed “quasi-judicial processes” were stopping wider cabinet discussions and input from the prime minister on issues of national importance.

Continue reading...
title: Morgan McSweeney calls for rethink of UK cabinet ministers’ ‘quasi-judicial’ powers

author: Flora Willson
description:
Barbican Hall, London
There was poise and passion in the Korean violinist’s Bartók, with Sakari Oramo and the BBC Symphony adding bite and touches of humour

In a classical music world where virtuosity comes as standard, only a handful of soloists find themselves regularly described as a “phenomenon”. Korean violinist Inmo Yang is among them – and he’s still on the rise, more than a decade after his first major competition win and three years since making his UK debut with the BBC Symphony Orchestra and their chief conductor Sakari Oramo. Reunited here with the same musicians for Bartók’s early Violin Concerto No 1, Yang was all poise and passion, delivering the long, winding paragraph for the soloist that opens the work
title: BBCSO/Oramo review – yes, Inmo Yang is phenomenal but the BBC Symphony shone even brighter tonight

author: Katherine Butler, associate editor, Europe
description:
Far-right populists remain insurgent and pro-EU governments are braced for Trump’s betrayal. But the midterms also showed that democracy can fight back

• Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

“Is Maga dead?” asked Margaret, a Guardian reader in Switzerland, in a live Q&A with our correspondents after the seismic US midterm elections. If Margaret’s query expressed a hope that the Democrats’ blue wave could transform Europe’s fortunes after two years of Maga-induced trauma, she was probably not alone.

The resounding defeat for Donald Trump’s Republicans and the installation of a Democratic-controlled US Congress has be
title: Is the US blue wave a turning point for Europe, too?

author: As told to Rhiannon Evans
description:
We asked 20 tweenagers what they already own, love and think would make great gifts. Turns out it’s Lego, dance mats and plenty of lotions and potions

• The best Christmas gifts for teenagers

Buying for someone in the tweenage years can be a balancing act: while some kids are still crafting, enjoying board games and deep into Lego, others have moved on to skincare and guitars.

So, in an effort to cover the whole range, I spoke to 20 tweens (from 10 to 12 years old) from across the country. But instead of asking what they want, I quizzed them on the things they already have, truly love and use regularly. Here are their tried and tested gift ideas for a range of prices.

Continue reading...
title: The 37 best Christmas gifts in the UK for tweens – chosen by 10- to 12-year-olds

author: Arifa Akbar
description:
National Theatre, London
The experimental 1979 drama gleefully muddles roles in a century-spanning caper that bounces from colonial Africa to hippy London

Caryl Churchill’s time-hopping 1979 drama is not revived as often as it might be, perhaps because it is so magnificently madcap. Bouncing from a first act satirising Victorian life in colonial Africa to a second act exploring sexual liberation in 1970s London, it could easily roll off-kilter in the wrong hands. There is also its complicated framework. Cloud 9 is a play in two distinct parts which follows some of the characters a century on, although they only age 25 years in that time and are played by different actors through ironic cross-casting.

Thankfully this crisp, handsome and note-perfect revival lands in exactly the right hands with director Dominic Cooke, clear as crystal despite the complications, sizzling with satire but showing itself to be a deadly serious, and still highly topic
title: Caryl Churchill’s magnificent Cloud 9 reaches for the skies – the National Theatre has done it proud

author: Tom Service
description:
Julian Lloyd Webber is the latest to decry the decline of UK music education. Why won’t politicians put the money where the mouth is? Plus, ENO drops its ‘E’

It’s been a big month for young talent. Barely a week after the final of BBC Young Musician, the next generation of musicians were also celebrated in the annual Music for Youth Proms at the Royal Albert Hall on Monday and Tuesday, where more than 2,000 young people in choirs, jazz and pop groups, steelpan bands and orchestras performed music that included Charlotte Harding’s The Orchestra: A Young Person’s Guide, written for disabled and non-disabled musicians of the National Open Youth Orchestra.

But amid the celebrations, there have been words of caution
title: Come on Andy… stop gaslighting us and fund music education

author: Martin Lewis
description:
There are thousands of small tips to make our country better. People know what is wrong, and it’s clear they have solutions

Have you ever come across an annoying little problem and thought, “why don’t they just fix that?” If so, I want to hear from you. I’m looking for your ideas for practical, low-cost, non-controversial ways to improve the UK – whether that’s health, schools, transport, business, housing, policing, justice, tech, shopping, money – or owt else entirely.

The spark for this happened just over a year ago, when I spoke at Politico’s fringe event at Labour’s conference. The key discussion was about Keir Starmer’s unpopularity. I was asked what I’d have advised the government when it took power, so I said: “Come up with 100 small things that piss people off and that you can fix, and they can see that you have fixed them.” Then I reeled off a list of small fixes for my subject area: the count
title: From blood group ID to cycle racks : I asked for little ways to fix broken Britain and the public’s ideas give me hope  | Martin Lewis

author: Lauren Almeida
description:
Ad revenue slowdown forces company to reduce spending on content by £25m before inquiry into takeover by Sky

  • Business live – latest updates

ITV plans to cut costs by £30m this year, as the TV sector faces a chill wind of ditched commissions, falling advertising sales and job reductions.

The broadcaster, which has agreed to sell its television and streaming business to Sky, expects ad revenues in that division to fall between 5% and 10% in the crucial final quarter of the year, despite the typically busy Christmas season.

Continue
title: ITV to cut costs by £30m amid falling advertising sales

author: Ashifa Kassam European community affairs correspondent
description:
Rights groups oppose new law that will let police forcibly enter homes to remove refused asylum seekers

Belgium could see ICE-style home raids, echoing the US crackdown on immigration, rights campaigners have warned, after MPs approved a law that allows police to forcibly enter properties to remove undocumented people.

For months, intense debate has swirled across Belgium over measures introduced by the ruling right-leaning coalition to ramp up expulsions of people who have been denied the right to stay in the country.

Continue reading...
title: Belgian plan for ICE-style immigration raids on homes criticised as ‘law of fear’

author: Maeve McClenaghan and Rachael Healy
description:
Multiple women have described unwanted sexual advances from the comedy star, allegations he denies

David Walliams, one of Britain’s best-known television personalities and top-selling children’s authors, has been accused of using his power and celebrity status to prey on young women and teenagers for sex.

The allegations, which span many years, were made in a joint investigation with ITV News into Walliams’ conduct towards young women.

Continue reading...
title: What is David Walliams accused of and what has he said in response?

author: Jessica Murray Social affairs correspondent
description:
Former shoplifters say treatment and drug rehabilitation are essential to ending cycle of theft and imprisonment

  • Police to target 500 chronic shoplifters in retail crime crackdown in England and Wales

When Rhys, 34, stole goods from shops across Birmingham, he would often leave notes for the staff apologising for his actions.

“I’d feel that guilty about it. I’d pass them notes, saying I’m so sorry about this,” he said. “But in the end, I was just that numb to it, and fearless as well. I’d walk in with a suitcase and ram everything into it, and not think twice about it.”

Continue reading...
title: ‘I’d steal 10-15 times a day’: ex-offenders on the addictions driving prolific shoplifting

author: Sandra Laville
description:
181GW of gas-fired capacity proposed for sites in US and Europe because of delays in connecting to national grids, says report

Developers of AI datacentres plan to build on-site climate-destroying gas power stations on a huge scale to meet their energy demands, research reveals.

Datacentres planned across the US, the UK and mainland Europe have proposals to build fossil fuel plants on-site to create 181GW of gas-fired capacity because of delays to connect to national grids, according to the findings. This is almost four times the total peak electricity demand of Great Britain.

Continue reading...
title: AI datacentres plan on-site power stations on huge scale despite climate risks, research reveals

author: Guardian sport
description:
• Danny Baker pays tribute to the ‘funniest man I knew’

  • Kelly was former editor of the NME and Q magazines

Danny Kelly, the renowned sport and music journalist, has died at the age of 69.

A statement from TalkSport, who he joined in 2007 and for whom he broadcast regularly until stepping away in March after being diagnosed with throat cancer, read: “We are heartbroken to share that our much-loved friend and colleague Danny Kelly has died, aged 69. A cherished part of talkSPORT for so many years, Danny brought extraordinary wit, warmth and knowledge to our airwaves. His passion for football, music and life was infectious, and his kindness touched everyone around him.

Continue reading...
title: Danny Kelly, football broadcaster and renowned editor, dies aged 69

author: Tanya Aldred
description:
Left-arm spinner who has died aged 78 played alongside Ian Botham and Viv Richards in county’s glory days, experience he passed on to Jos Buttler and many others

Away from the bright lights and the hungry eye of television, cricket unfolds as it has always done, with a quiet welcoming handshake across the generations. Dennis Breakwell was the quintessence of that.

Breakwell died this week at the age of 78, after a 15-year career as a slow left-arm bowler at Northamptonshire and Somerset, and more than 20 years as a groundsman and coach at King’s College Taunton. There he cut the grass, watched, and became a touchstone for generations of young cricketers passing through the school, including Jos Buttler.

This is an extract from the Guardian’s weekly cricket email, The Spin. To subscribe, just visit this page and follow the instructions.
title: Farewell Dennis Breakwell, Somerset stalwart and mentor to generations of cricketers

author: Guardian community team
description:
We’d like to hear from private renters about rising costs, finding somewhere to live and dealing with landlords

Private renters are facing steep rent rises and a shortage of affordable properties, with growing numbers of landlords selling up. The Renters’ Rights Act, which came into force in England in May, introduced new protections for tenants, but many continue to face uncertainty about their housing.

While some renters have successfully secured reductions, others are struggling with soaring costs and a highly competitive rental market. Meanwhile England’s housing courts have been overloaded with renters battling evictions<
title: Private renters in the UK: how difficult is the rental market where you live?

author: Matt Hughes
description:
• Wage bills in third tier have increased by 15% this season

  • ‘Luxury tax’ and three-year limits on losses considered

League One clubs want to introduce new spending restrictions to reduce losses by limiting investment from owners.

Clubs in the division voted to tighten the rules last summer by reducing spending limits from 60% to 50% of turnover, and removed a staggered approach to owner investment, so that only 50% of equity injections can be spent on squad costs, with the rest assigned to infrastructure projects. Less than six months later many want to go further.

Continue reading...
title: League One clubs aim for further curbs on spending as budgets continue to spiral

author: Sali Hughes
description:
Bioderma’s new eczema lotion will be comforting for anyone with dry skin. Plus another brilliant problem solving mosituriser

I spent much of my childhood basted in crude, heavy-duty emollient creams and grim bath oils. But few patients are as short-changed as eczema sufferers, whose treatments and regimens are not only joyless, but sometimes provide little reward for the trouble.

Although unctuous emollients are necessary to protect a compromised skin barrier, they have a habit of just “sitting” there greasily, refusing to sink in or curtail the itch. The French pharmaceutical brand Bioderma is finally advancing the conversation. Its extensive research into eczema, as well as a recent study of 500 sufferers (about one in five children and one in 10 adults struggle with the condition), were presented as a breakthrough in eczema care at last month’s EADV (European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology) conference in Vienna.
title: Sali Hughes on beauty: a lotion to cure autumn dryness – and relieve eczema sufferers’ sore skin

author: Heather Stewart
description:
Kemi Badenoch attacked reforms but is not being clear about how party would meet costs, Torsten Bell claims

Kemi Badenoch’s Conservatives would have to raise the state pension age above 70 to meet the cost of keeping the triple lock, Treasury minister Torsten Bell has claimed.

Labour has announced reforms to the triple-lock promise to come into force in the next parliament – with the initial proceeds earmarked for Andy Burnham’s national care service.

Continue reading...
title: Tories would have to raise state pension age above 70 to keep triple lock, says minister

author: Ajit Niranjan
description:
Third day of UN talks begin but leaders of many big polluting nations absent

As day three of the UN climate summit kicks off, world leaders from dozens of countries are expected. But heads of government from Canada, Japan and across Europe have got lost on the road, civil society observers report.

Today is the Cop31 leaders’ summit in Antalya, where world leaders are supposed to appear, hear each others’ concerns and pledge their commitment to solving the climate crisis.

Continue reading...
title: Cop31 live: World leaders to speak at climate crisis summit

author: Zoe Wood
description:
Industry experts pick out tiny turntable as one of their ‘15 hottest toys’ for the festive season

A record player so small it belongs at a party in a Barbie Dreamhouse is one of this year’s must-have Christmas gifts as the vinyl revival takes an unexpected turn.

The £19.99 micro music set plays dinky 1.5in records and comes with an exclusive “mini vinyl” of the school disco favourite APT by Rosé and Bruno Mars. The toy makes the Toy Retailers Association’s annual DreamToys list of the 15 “hottest toys” this festive season.

Continue reading...
title: Mini record player on track for No 1 in Christmas toy parade

author: Emily Bratt
description:
My romance with Steven quickly fizzled, but I had gained something just as good. It made me realise that in the endless, exhausting pursuit of love I had closed myself off to other kinds of connection

This autumn is my third anniversary with Steven. In October 2023, we matched on Bumble when I was in his home town of Atlanta for a wedding. We met for dinner downtown and even though we’re from different countries, we discovered a mutual love for the British comedy show Stath Lets Flats. It was a done deal.

But Steven isn’t my partner, he’s my friend. And if we’re being teenage about it, I’d probably brand him one of my best, despite living 4,000 miles away. Over the past three years, we’ve visited each other’s homes, holidayed together and met one another’s friends and family. I’ve even had dinner with his ex-wife, whom I also now consider a friend. Steven and I have all the hallmarks of a perfect relationship. We just don’t fancy each other.
title: A moment that changed me: a failed date led to one of the greatest friendships of my life

author: Hollie Richardson, Phil Harrison, Jack Seale, Ali Catterall and Simon Wardell
description:
Hunting Alice Bell is a twisty drama by Peter Bradshaw and David Baddiel. Plus, Ken Loach on Cathy Come Home. Here’s what to watch this evening

9pm, Channel 4
Fran (Alexandra Roach) is a suburban mum working at a leisure centre. When she makes a video for her work’s website, it goes viral for the wrong reasons: trolls believe they have worked out that she is, in fact, Alice Bell, a former nurse who helped her anaesthetist serial killer boyfriend, Jason (Simon Pegg), then resumed life with a new identity. As events unravel, Fran learns she’s not the only woman who has been forced to deny she is Bell. But who is telling the truth? Is one of them lying? Created by David Baddiel and the Guardian’s chief film critic, Peter Bradshaw, it’s a nightmare that, in this AI world, never feels too far-fetched. Hollie Richardson
title: TV tonight: a nightmarish thriller about a group of women accused of an awful crime

author: David Hytner
description:
Obsessive attention to detail is helping striker to reach new heights – and a 126th international appearance on Thursday

It was Harry Kane’s dirty little secret. Something the England captain got up to after matches. He felt he deserved the indulgence. Yes, it can be revealed, Kane loved to reward himself after a gruelling 90 minutes with a bag of sweets. “I do like a Haribo,” he said with a smile after the Nations League win against Czechia in Prague at the end of September.

No more. At the beginning of last season, Kane took the decision to cut out the naughty treats. After a while, he noticed a difference. He felt sharper; able to sprint more, make a greater number of accelerations. Was it down to this latest entry on the list of personal sacrifices? Or was it a consequence of his broader health regime, the scope of which is mind-bl
title: Bone broth, sweets ban and acupuncture: Harry Kane’s road to record England cap

author: Ranie Saidi
description:
Leeks play a major part in two Malaysian-inspired dishes: they melt into coconut in a marvellous chicken curry, and pair perfectly with peas in crunchy potato croquettes

Since moving from Malaysia to London more than a decade ago, I’ve slowly brought leeks into my everyday cooking. Their gentle sweetness reminds me of banana shallots, and I love how they melt into this chicken gulai. Bergedil (or begedil or perkedel) have always been one of my favourite street-food snacks, and are found at stalls across Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia. In Malay cooking, they’re often made using mashed potato that’s mixed with minced meat, shaped and fried, but my version uses leeks, frozen peas and leftover herbs, plus an orange, chilli and yoghurt dip.

Continue reading...
title: Chicken curry and potato croquettes: Ranie Saidi’s recipes for a Malaysian feast

author: Mike Hytner
description:
• Book tour will still go ahead but with changes this week’s schedule

  • Khawaja evasive when questioned on ABC’s 7:30 Report

Usman Khawaja’s promotional book tour has been subject to “adjustments” after the former Australia Test batter was grilled about certain claims on the ABC’s 7.30 Report.

Khawaja pulled out of some radio and television spots on Wednesday, with his publisher Penguin saying that while the tour had not been cancelled entirely, changes had been made to his schedule this week.

Continue reading...
title: Usman Khawaja bunkers down as book tour ‘adjusted’ amid ball-tampering claims

author: Guardian staff and agencies
description:
Ukrainian president dismisses Moscow’s claims of gains in Donbas region but says first day of trilateral talks were constructive. What we know on day 1,722

Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the US has backed Ukraine’s assessment of what is happening on the battlefield and that Vladimir Putin lives in a “different reality”, as American-led trilateral discussions between Ukraine, ⁠Russia and the US got under way in Abu Dhabi. In a post on social media, Zelenskyy said that Russia has claimed at the talks that they occupied half of the Donbas in Ukraine’s east. “This is the problem. Putin lives in a different reality,” the Ukrainian president wrote, adding “I can draw a picture for him too where I fully occupy Russia. But it’s not true. What was good is that the American side confirmed the Ukrainian assessment of what is happening on the battlefield.”

Zelenskyy said he was “happy” to see a change in the approach by US mediators
title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy says Putin ‘lives in a different reality’ as Abu Dhabi talks get under way
